title: Xinzuo Academy
subtitle: Interactive staff training from The Gongfu of Xinzuo

levels.title: Base
levels.purpose: Recognize the full map of kitchen-knife knowledge and apply safe, correct first principles across every major theme of The Gongfu of Xinzuo.

modules.title: Anatomy & Construction
modules.summary: Name the main parts and understand basic construction terms without turning them into quality slogans.

lessons.title: Blade anatomy and the cutting edge

content.lead: Accurate knife knowledge starts by naming the parts correctly.
points: The spine is the normally unsharpened upper side; the heel is the rear of the cutting edge.
The cutting edge — in this guide, filo and tagliente are synonyms — is the sharpened boundary of the blade.
A bevel is the sloping geometry that leads toward the apex; surface finish is a separate characteristic.
content.takeaway: First identify the feature; then explain what it does.

question.prompt: Which term names the rear part of the cutting edge?

options.text: Heel
Spine
Tip
Bolster

question.explanation: The heel is the rear section of the sharpened edge, close to the handle.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates bevel from finish?

options.text: Bevel and finish are two names for the same feature.
Finish sets the tang type; bevel sets the handle shape.
Bevel describes geometry; finish describes the blade surface.
Finish is the edge angle; bevel is only decoration.

recovery_questions.explanation: Geometry and surface appearance must not be confused.

lessons.title: Tang, bolster and construction

content.lead: Construction terms describe how the knife is built; they do not create an automatic quality ranking.
points: A full tang follows most of the handle outline; a hidden tang is enclosed inside the handle.
A through tang reaches the butt but is not simply another name for a full tang.
Forging describes a manufacturing step, not a guarantee of superior geometry, heat treatment or finish.
content.takeaway: Judge the complete construction, not one label.

question.prompt: What does a full tang mainly describe?

options.text: How hard the cutting edge has been heat treated
How many layers are visible on the blade face
How symmetrical the edge bevel has been ground
How far the blade steel extends through the handle

question.explanation: Tang terminology describes handle construction, not hardness or bevel geometry.

recovery_questions.prompt: A knife has a welded bolster. What can that fact prove by itself?

options.text: Only how that part was assembled, not overall quality
That the blade steel is automatically low grade
That the knife cannot have good heat treatment
That the edge geometry must be thick and robust

recovery_questions.explanation: A construction detail must be evaluated together with execution and the rest of the knife.

questions.prompt: Where is the cutting edge?

options.text: Along the normally blunt spine
Along the sharpened boundary of the blade
Inside the handle around the tang
Only at the front tip of the knife

questions.explanation: The cutting edge is the sharpened boundary, not the spine or handle.

questions.prompt: Which statement about forging is sound?

options.text: It guarantees a thinner edge than every stamped blade.
It guarantees higher hardness regardless of steel choice.
It is a process step; final quality still depends on many other factors.
It guarantees a full tang and a welded bolster together.

questions.explanation: Forging alone cannot establish the final performance of a knife.

modules.title: Steel Properties
modules.summary: Use a five-dimension framework instead of judging steel by HRC or a single marketing claim.

lessons.title: The five dimensions of knife steel

content.lead: Steel performance is a balance of properties, not a single number.
points: The five teaching dimensions are hardness, sharpening response, corrosion resistance, toughness and microstructural fineness.
HRC measures resistance to permanent deformation; it does not directly measure sharpness or overall quality.
The useful balance depends on the knife, the task and the user.
content.takeaway: Do not rank steels by one property alone.

question.prompt: Which property is measured by HRC?

options.text: Sharpness
Hardness
Toughness
Corrosion resistance

question.explanation: Rockwell C is a hardness scale; the other properties require different evidence.

recovery_questions.prompt: Two steels have the same HRC. What is the safest conclusion?

options.text: They must hold an edge for exactly the same time.
They must contain the same carbide population.
They must resist corrosion to the same degree.
They can still differ in wear, toughness and sharpening response.

recovery_questions.explanation: Hardness is only one part of steel behaviour.

lessons.title: Stainless does not mean maintenance-free

content.lead: Corrosion resistance and sharpening response are both system properties.
points: Stainless classification commonly starts at about 10.5% chromium by mass, but corrosion resistance still varies widely.
Chromium supports passivation; salt, acids and prolonged wetness can still stain or pit stainless steel.
The shortcut 'softer steel is easier to sharpen' is unreliable because matrix and carbides also control abrasion and burr behaviour.
content.takeaway: Stainless is corrosion-resistant, not stain-proof.

question.prompt: Which statement about stainless knife steel is correct?

options.text: It cannot stain if chromium exceeds the stainless threshold.
It never needs attention after acidic or salty foods.
It resists corrosion but still benefits from prompt cleaning and drying.
Its corrosion resistance is determined by HRC alone.

question.explanation: Stainless steels vary, and normal care still matters.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a harder carbon steel sometimes sharpen cleanly on water stones?

options.text: Hardness automatically makes every abrasive cut faster.
Sharpening response also depends on microstructure, carbides and burr behaviour.
Carbon steel contains no hard particles at all.
Water stones ignore hardness once they are wet.

recovery_questions.explanation: Hardness alone does not predict sharpening feel.

questions.prompt: What is the best first question when comparing steels?

options.text: Which balance of properties suits this use?
Which steel has the highest HRC number?
Which steel has the longest alloying list?
Which steel has the most expensive name?

questions.explanation: Steel selection begins from use and trade-offs, not a single prestige signal.

questions.prompt: What does passivation mainly do?

options.text: Turns the entire blade into a harder martensitic phase
Removes every carbide from the steel matrix
Makes the edge angle smaller during normal use
Forms a thin protective oxide layer at the surface

questions.explanation: Passivation slows corrosion at the surface; it is not a hardening process.

modules.title: Metallurgy & Heat Treatment
modules.summary: Understand the basic chain from composition to microstructure, heat treatment and powder metallurgy.

lessons.title: Alloying elements create possibilities

content.lead: Chemical composition matters, but it is the starting point rather than the complete performance specification.
points: Carbon enables high hardness; chromium supports stainless behaviour; molybdenum can aid hardenability and pitting resistance.
Vanadium, tungsten and niobium can form very hard carbides that raise wear resistance but may slow sharpening.
More alloying is not automatically better because elements interact with heat treatment and microstructure.
content.takeaway: Composition defines potential; processing turns it into performance.

question.prompt: What is the safest use of an alloy composition table?

options.text: Use it as one input together with heat treatment and geometry.
Use it to rank every knife without looking at construction.
Use the number of elements as a direct quality score.
Use chromium percentage as a complete cutting-performance rating.

question.explanation: Composition alone does not determine the finished knife.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which element is most directly associated with stainless passivation?

options.text: Tungsten
Cobalt
Chromium
Vanadium

recovery_questions.explanation: Chromium is the central alloying element behind stainless passivation.

lessons.title: Heat treatment, carbides and powder metallurgy

content.lead: Steel chemistry must be converted into a useful microstructure by processing and heat treatment.
points: Austenitizing prepares the high-temperature phase; quenching forms hard martensitic structure; tempering makes that structure usable.
Retained austenite can be reduced by suitable sub-zero or deep-freeze processing in demanding steels.
Powder metallurgy can improve uniformity and carbide distribution compared with conventional solidification, especially in highly alloyed steels.
content.takeaway: Steelmaking route and heat treatment shape the microstructure you actually cut with.

question.prompt: What is the main purpose of tempering after hardening?

options.text: Add chromium to the steel after the blade is finished
Create the handle material around the finished tang
Turn a double bevel into a single bevel by heating
Make the hardened structure usable by adjusting its properties

question.explanation: Tempering follows hardening to balance the final martensitic structure.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is powder metallurgy useful in high-alloy steels?

options.text: It can produce a finer, more uniform distribution of alloy-rich particles.
It removes the need for any later heat treatment.
It guarantees that every powder steel is tougher than every conventional steel.
It makes carbide type irrelevant to sharpening behaviour.

recovery_questions.explanation: Powder metallurgy changes solidification and distribution; it does not eliminate trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What can very hard carbides generally increase?

options.text: Handle moisture resistance
Abrasive wear resistance
Blade length during sharpening
Tang size inside the handle

questions.explanation: Hard carbides can improve wear resistance, with sharpening trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Which phase is the hard structure sought by quenching knife steel?

options.text: Austenite
Ferrite
Martensite
Graphite

questions.explanation: Quenching is used to form martensitic structure from the high-temperature condition.

modules.title: Xinzuo Steels & Handle Materials
modules.summary: Recognize the main material families and explain them as design choices rather than rankings.

lessons.title: Read the Xinzuo steel range by design goal

content.lead: The Xinzuo range uses different steels because different knives and users need different balances.
points: Premium powder steels such as ZDP-189, SRS13 and M390 pursue different combinations of hardness, wear resistance and corrosion behaviour.
10Cr15CoMoV, 12Cr18MoV, AUS-10, VG10 and 14C28N occupy different all-round stainless positions rather than one simple ranking.
Blue Steel No. 2 trades stainless convenience for responsive carbon-steel behaviour; 1.4116 occupies a more forgiving moderate-hardness position.
content.takeaway: Choose the balance, not the most prestigious steel name.

question.prompt: Which statement best describes the Xinzuo steel range?

options.text: Every newer steel is automatically better for every customer.
Different steels target different balances of properties and use.
HRC alone determines which steel belongs at the top.
Carbon steels are always easier choices than stainless steels.

question.explanation: The range is deliberately diverse because needs differ.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is the basic trade-off of Blue Steel No. 2 in this range?

options.text: Complete rust immunity in exchange for very low hardness
No sharpening response in exchange for maximum chromium
Very soft matrix in exchange for a ceramic-like handle
Reactive carbon-steel care in exchange for responsive sharpening behaviour

recovery_questions.explanation: Blue Steel No. 2 is valued for carbon-steel behaviour, with corresponding care needs.

lessons.title: Handle materials change feel and care

content.lead: A handle material should be judged by how it changes the complete knife, not by prestige alone.
points: Technical materials such as PP, ABS, G10 and carbon-fibre composites emphasize different balances of moisture resistance, weight and feel.
Micarta, pakka wood and stabilized wood combine fibres or wood with resins to change stability and maintenance.
Natural woods vary in density, grain and care needs; material name alone does not establish ergonomics or quality.
content.takeaway: Material, shape, surface, weight and care must be evaluated together.

question.prompt: What should staff avoid when describing a handle material?

options.text: Explaining how moisture resistance can affect daily use
Comparing weight and surface feel between suitable handles
Treating the material name alone as a complete quality score
Discussing different care needs for natural and technical materials

question.explanation: Handle quality depends on design, execution and fit as well as material.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a denser handle material change knife feel?

options.text: It automatically changes the chemical composition of the blade.
It can move mass rearward and alter perceived balance.
It forces the cutting edge into a single-bevel geometry.
It removes the need to compare handle shape and circumference.

recovery_questions.explanation: Handle material contributes to mass distribution but does not replace ergonomic evaluation.

mini_test.title: Quick check · Xinzuo Steels & Handle Materials

questions.prompt: When should staff compare exact steel grades?

options.text: After identifying knives whose function already suits the customer
Before asking what the customer cuts or how they work
Instead of checking blade geometry or intended use
Only after choosing the most decorative blade pattern

questions.explanation: Steel is a differentiator among suitable knives, not a substitute for suitability.

questions.prompt: Which handle choice is most defensible?

options.text: The rarest material regardless of grip or working environment
The heaviest handle regardless of the blade's balance
The hardest surface regardless of comfort during repeated use
The one whose material, shape and care fit the user's needs

questions.explanation: The complete hand interface matters more than a material label.

modules.title: Damascus & Layered Construction
modules.summary: Distinguish real layered construction from decoration and understand differential wear without marketing shortcuts.

lessons.title: Layered Damascus versus surface decoration

content.lead: A visible Damascus-like pattern does not, by itself, tell you how the blade was built.
points: Pattern-welded Damascus is created from real layers joined and manipulated through the blade construction.
Laser or other surface decoration can imitate a pattern without creating a layered structure.
Layer count can describe construction complexity, but it is not a direct sharpness or quality score.
content.takeaway: First identify the construction; only then discuss the pattern.

question.prompt: What best distinguishes genuine layered Damascus from a laser pattern?

options.text: The pattern comes from joined material layers rather than surface marking.
The genuine blade always has the highest HRC in the range.
The genuine blade always contains more chromium than any monosteel.
The laser pattern can be identified only by the handle material.

question.explanation: Construction, not visual complexity alone, defines layered Damascus.

recovery_questions.prompt: What does a higher layer count prove on its own?

options.text: A sharper apex regardless of sharpening and edge geometry
Greater toughness regardless of steel and heat treatment
More layers in the stated construction, not automatically better cutting
Higher corrosion resistance regardless of alloy composition

recovery_questions.explanation: Layer count is descriptive; performance still follows the complete design.

lessons.title: Full Damascus and differential wear

content.lead: Full-Damascus blades can develop a changing microscopic edge texture as different layers wear at different rates.
points: Differential wear can preserve slicing bite even as peak sharpness gradually declines.
This is not literal automatic sharpening and it does not remove the need for maintenance.
Sharpness and slicing bite are related but not identical sensations.
content.takeaway: Differential wear changes edge character; it does not create a maintenance-free knife.

question.prompt: What can differential wear in full Damascus help preserve?

options.text: A perfectly polished apex without any future sharpening
The exact factory angle regardless of how the knife is used
Complete immunity to chipping under lateral loads
Slicing bite as the microscopic edge texture evolves

question.explanation: The effect concerns edge texture and slicing behaviour, not automatic restoration of factory geometry.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is 'self-sharpening' potentially misleading for full Damascus?

options.text: The edge still wears and eventually needs normal maintenance.
The blade cannot develop any microscopic texture during use.
The layers all wear at exactly the same rate by definition.
The effect exists only on laser-decorated monosteel blades.

recovery_questions.explanation: Differential wear may change bite, but it is not perpetual sharpening.

questions.prompt: Which term should Italian staff reserve for a monosteel blade with a laser-applied Damascus-like pattern?

options.text: Acciaio Damasco stratificato
Damascato superficialmente
Damasco integrale saldato
Pacchetto Damasco strutturale

questions.explanation: In this guide 'damascato' is reserved for surface decoration, not genuine layered Damascus.

questions.prompt: Which two ideas should be kept separate?

options.text: Blade length and handle colour
Tang shape and packaging size
Peak sharpness and slicing bite
Logo position and Rockwell scale

questions.explanation: A toothier edge can keep useful slicing bite even when peak refinement changes.

modules.title: Geometry & Bevels
modules.summary: Recognize the main bevel families and the basic consequences of symmetry, asymmetry and single-bevel construction.

lessons.title: Read bevel families as geometry

content.lead: Bevel names describe how steel supports and guides the edge; they are not quality rankings.
points: Common families include symmetrical V, convex, asymmetric V, compound V, hollow, single-sided and single-sided with urasuki.
A compound edge separates the broad primary geometry from the small edge bevel used in routine sharpening.
Strength and cutting resistance depend on thickness, angle, steel and support, not simply on bevel count.
content.takeaway: Read the cross-section before making claims about behaviour.

question.prompt: Which part is normally restored in routine sharpening of a compound double-V edge?

options.text: The entire broad primary grind every time
The small edge bevel at the apex
The spine thickness along the full blade
The tang surface inside the handle scales

question.explanation: Routine sharpening restores the edge bevel; thinning the primary geometry is a different operation.

recovery_questions.prompt: Does a double bevel always mean a perfect 50/50 geometry?

options.text: Yes; any asymmetry would make it a single bevel.
Yes; only handle geometry can be asymmetric.
No; because double bevel means the spine is sharpened too.
No; both sides are sharpened, but the proportions can differ.

recovery_questions.explanation: Bevel count and exact symmetry are separate properties.

lessons.title: Single bevel, urasuki and steering

content.lead: Strong asymmetry can create handedness and directional behaviour that must be checked model by model.
points: A traditional single-bevel knife places the main bevel on one side; many specialist forms use an urasuki hollow on the reverse.
The urasuki is a functional hollow with narrow reference lands, not an unfinished back surface.
Sharpening must preserve the existing geometry; do not turn the reverse into a normal double-bevel facet.
content.takeaway: Check the exact grind and lateral orientation before advising use or sharpening.

question.prompt: What is the urasuki on a traditional single-bevel knife?

options.text: A decorative laser pattern on the main bevel
A second normal edge bevel at the same angle
A shallow functional hollow on the reverse face
A full tang visible along the handle outline

question.explanation: The urasuki is part of the specialist working geometry.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a strongly asymmetric edge steer?

options.text: The handle colour changes friction at the cutting edge.
The two sides displace food differently as the blade advances.
The HRC number pulls the blade toward the harder side.
The tang becomes magnetized by repeated sharpening.

recovery_questions.explanation: Directional behaviour comes from asymmetric working geometry.

questions.prompt: What can a convex section generally change compared with a similar flat section?

options.text: How material supports the edge and separates food
Whether the steel becomes stainless during use
Whether the tang reaches the end of the handle
Whether the knife was packed in a wooden box

questions.explanation: Cross-section geometry influences support and cutting interaction.

questions.prompt: Before giving handedness advice, what should staff verify?

options.text: Only the silhouette and country of origin
Only the handle material and blade length
Only whether the blade has a Damascus pattern
The exact model's grind and orientation

questions.explanation: A traditional profile name alone does not prove the exact grind.

modules.title: Knife Families & Ergonomics
modules.summary: Match blade families to tasks and understand how weight, balance and grip affect the choice.

lessons.title: Choose knife families by work

content.lead: Knife names are useful only when they connect to the mechanical work a blade is designed to do.
points: Chef's knife, gyuto, santoku, bunka and many Chinese cleavers can be multi-use tools with different profiles and movement preferences.
Boning, filleting, fish butchery and long slicing need specialist geometries rather than simply more force.
Bread, frozen food and other hard-food tasks can require serrated or dedicated tools.
content.takeaway: Start from the work; then choose the knife family.

question.prompt: What should staff identify before recommending a blade family?

options.text: The foods, quantities and cutting movements involved
The most decorative pattern currently in stock
The highest hardness number on the product list
The most expensive handle material in the display

question.explanation: Functional requirements come before appearance or prestige.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which statement about a thin Chinese cleaver is safest?

options.text: Every Chinese cleaver is intended for heavy bone impact.
Every Chinese cleaver must use single-bevel geometry.
It can be a board-oriented multi-use knife and not a bone chopper.
Every Chinese cleaver is unsuitable for vegetable work.

recovery_questions.explanation: The family name does not override the exact geometry and intended use.

lessons.title: Weight, balance and grip change handling

content.lead: Two knives with similar steel and geometry can feel very different because mass distribution and grip change leverage.
points: More mass can add momentum but also needs more effort to start, stop and redirect.
Blade-forward, neutral and rearward balance feel different even at the same total weight.
Moving from a handle grip toward a pinch grip changes perceived balance because the hand moves closer to blade mass.
content.takeaway: Evaluate balance in the user's real grip, not from a specification sheet alone.

question.prompt: Why can the same knife feel better balanced in a pinch grip?

options.text: The blade physically becomes lighter when touched forward.
The steel hardness falls when the hand crosses the bolster.
The tang shortens as the hand moves toward the blade.
The controlling fingers move closer to the blade's mass.

question.explanation: Grip position changes leverage, not the knife's actual mass.

recovery_questions.prompt: Two suitable knives weigh the same but feel different. What should staff compare?

options.text: Mass distribution, handle shape and the customer's grip
Only the printed total weight on the product card
Only the country in which the steel was developed
Only the number of decorative layers in the blade

recovery_questions.explanation: Ergonomic fit depends on where mass and the hand meet.

questions.prompt: Why is a long slicer long?

options.text: To increase sideways leverage around hard joints
To use more edge in a smooth drawing cut
To make the knife suitable for striking frozen food
To move the balance as far behind the handle as possible

questions.explanation: Length helps when the cutting movement actually uses that edge length.

questions.prompt: What is the correct recommendation sequence?

options.text: Appearance → hardness → function
Price → pattern → handle length
Function → ergonomics → selection
Steel grade → box → cutting task

questions.explanation: Solve the work first, then fit, then select among suitable products.

modules.title: Cutting Techniques
modules.summary: Recognize the main movement paths and use specialist techniques without forcing the blade.

lessons.title: Recognize the main cutting paths

content.lead: Technique begins by observing the path of the edge rather than memorizing labels.
points: Direct descent suits fairly flat edge sections; an advancing stroke combines forward and downward travel.
Long slicing uses a draw through the food, spreading work across more edge length.
Rocking keeps a changing contact point and works best with suitable belly curvature.
content.takeaway: Choose a movement that matches edge shape and food instead of forcing the knife.

question.prompt: Which movement adds forward travel while the blade descends?

options.text: Pure direct descent
Advancing push cut
Static in-hand peeling
Sideways board scraping

question.explanation: The advancing stroke combines slicing travel with descent.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why does a long drawing stroke help a slicer?

options.text: It increases sideways pressure so the blade can lever food apart.
It keeps one point of the tip fixed on the board at all times.
It makes edge geometry irrelevant once enough speed is reached.
It spreads the cut over more edge and reduces repeated sawing.

recovery_questions.explanation: Long slicing works because the stroke actually uses the available edge length.

lessons.title: Use specialist movements within their limits

content.lead: Fine work, bone work, filleting and in-hand tasks require control rather than extra force.
points: The supporting hand should be set before the blade moves, with fingertips protected from the cutting path.
Work around bones and joints follows anatomy; do not use a fine blade as a lever.
Filleting follows contours with only the flex designed into the knife; specialist techniques that need demonstration should not be improvised.
content.takeaway: Control the path first; force is never a substitute for fit.

question.prompt: When should the supporting hand be positioned?

options.text: After the first cut reveals the blade path
Only when cutting very small ingredients
Before the knife starts moving
Only when using a forward pinch grip

question.explanation: Hand position establishes the safe path before movement.

recovery_questions.prompt: A hard fillet knife reaches its natural flex limit. What should the user do?

options.text: Twist the handle until the blade follows the contour.
Change the cutting angle rather than forcing more bend.
Lever against the bones to increase the available bend.
Strike the spine so the blade flexes through the section.

recovery_questions.explanation: Use only the flex the model is designed to provide.

questions.prompt: A very flat edge leaves uncut skins during pure rocking. What is the likely issue?

options.text: The movement does not match the blade curvature well.
The handle material is absorbing too much moisture.
The steel contains too little chromium for the board.
The tang is too long for a repeated cutting motion.

questions.explanation: Technique should follow the geometry of the edge.

questions.prompt: What is the safest principle when working around a joint?

options.text: Increase force until the blade crosses the hard point.
Use lateral twist to separate every resistant section.
Hold the food in the air to improve access to the joint.
Follow the anatomy with controlled cuts instead of prying.

questions.explanation: A knife cuts; it should not be used as a pry bar.

modules.title: Safe Use & Handling
modules.summary: Make safety a complete system from workstation setup through washing, carrying and storage.

lessons.title: Build safety before the cut

content.lead: Most safe knife handling is decided before the blade starts moving.
points: Stable board, stable food, clear cutting path and protected fingertips form the basic pre-cut check.
Use the right knife for the task and only the force the cut requires.
Avoid twisting, sideways levering and scraping the board with the cutting edge.
content.takeaway: If the setup is unstable, the cut is not ready.

question.prompt: A round ingredient rolls on the board. What comes first?

options.text: Create a stable flat support before the main cut.
Grip it harder with exposed fingertips near the blade.
Use a faster stroke so the food has less time to move.
Choose a heavier knife and increase downward pressure.

question.explanation: Mechanical stability should be corrected before adding movement or force.

recovery_questions.prompt: A thin hard blade binds in dense food. What is the safe response?

options.text: Twist the handle gently until the food opens.
Use the blade face as a lever to widen the gap.
Withdraw it carefully and change the cut.
Strike the spine while keeping the blade trapped.

recovery_questions.explanation: Twisting creates damaging lateral load; change the cut instead.

lessons.title: Keep control when cutting stops

content.lead: Washing, passing, carrying and storage are still knife-handling tasks.
points: Never hide a sharp knife under soapy water or among objects in a sink.
Pass the handle deliberately; for short movement carry the knife low, still and with a predictable path.
If a knife falls, do not try to catch it; step away and let it fall.
content.takeaway: A knife must remain visible, controlled and predictable even when it is not cutting.

question.prompt: A knife slips from the counter. What should you do?

options.text: Catch the handle before the blade reaches the floor.
Block the blade with a foot to protect the edge.
Reach with both hands so one can stop the knife.
Move away and let it fall.

question.explanation: Trying to catch a falling knife creates an unnecessary injury risk.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which washing habit is unsafe?

options.text: Leaving the knife hidden in a sink of soapy water
Washing one knife at a time with the edge visible
Keeping the handle controlled while cleaning the blade
Drying the blade and handle promptly after rinsing

recovery_questions.explanation: Hidden blades can injure someone who reaches into the sink.

questions.prompt: Which is part of the four-point safety check?

options.text: Maximum downward force
Clear blade path
Wet cutting board surface
Exposed guiding fingertips

questions.explanation: A clear path is one of the basic pre-cut conditions.

questions.prompt: How should a knife be passed to another person?

options.text: Quickly, with the blade presented so it stays visible
Wrapped loosely in a towel with no clear orientation
Deliberately, with the handle presented and edge controlled
Balanced flat on the open palm while both people move

questions.explanation: Predictable orientation and control reduce transfer risk.

modules.title: Care & Cutting Boards
modules.summary: Protect the edge and materials through suitable boards, cleaning, drying, storage and appropriate maintenance.

lessons.title: Choose cutting boards by edge interaction

content.lead: The cutting board is part of the edge system because every board cut ends in surface contact.
points: Suitable wood, purpose-made plastic and resilient synthetic boards can be edge-friendly when clean, flat and stable.
End-grain wood lets fibres separate and recover more readily under the edge than many harder surfaces.
Glass, stone, ceramic and metal are too unyielding for routine work with fine kitchen edges.
content.takeaway: Judge a board by what it does to the edge as well as hygiene and care.

question.prompt: Which surface should be avoided for routine cutting with a fine edge?

options.text: Suitable wood
Glass
Purpose-made plastic
Resilient synthetic board

question.explanation: Glass is hard and unyielding at the moment of edge contact.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can end-grain wood be gentle on an edge?

options.text: It is harder than glass and therefore stops the edge sooner.
It chemically hardens the apex during every board contact.
It prevents all moisture from entering any type of wood.
Its fibre orientation can let fibres separate under the edge.

recovery_questions.explanation: Fibre orientation is one reason end grain can be edge-friendly.

lessons.title: Routine care is mostly prevention

content.lead: Good maintenance removes avoidable moisture, corrosion, impact and edge-contact risks.
points: Wash by hand, rinse salt and acids promptly, and dry blade and handle completely.
Carbon steel may develop a stable dark patina; active orange rust is different and should be addressed.
A honing rod can realign or maintain some edges, but it does not replace sharpening when the apex needs material removal.
content.takeaway: Prevent damage early instead of repairing it later.

question.prompt: What should happen after cutting salty or acidic food?

options.text: Leave the residue until the next normal washing cycle.
Soak the blade overnight to dissolve the remaining residue.
Rinse promptly and dry the knife completely.
Store the knife wet so the passive layer can form faster.

question.explanation: Removing salts, acids and moisture reduces unnecessary corrosion risk.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which statement about patina on carbon steel is correct?

options.text: Any colour change means the blade has structurally failed.
A stable dark patina is different from active orange rust.
Orange rust is a protective patina that should be preserved.
Patina proves the steel has become stainless during use.

recovery_questions.explanation: Patina and active rust are chemically and practically different conditions.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to compare board materials?

options.text: Compare edge friendliness, stability, hygiene and maintenance.
Choose the hardest surface because it lasts longest.
Choose only by whether the board can enter a dishwasher.
Choose only by appearance and ignore surface hardness.

questions.explanation: Board materials involve several practical trade-offs.

questions.prompt: When is a honing rod not a substitute for sharpening?

options.text: Whenever the handle is made from a technical composite
Whenever the knife is stored in a fitted blade guard
Whenever the cutting board is made from end-grain wood
When the apex needs abrasive material removal to be restored

questions.explanation: Honing and sharpening are different maintenance operations.

modules.title: Sharpening & Edge Maintenance
modules.summary: Build a repeatable basic process from stone setup and bevel contact through burr control and testing.

lessons.title: Set up the stone and verify contact

content.lead: Good sharpening begins with a stable, suitable stone and visible control of the edge bevel.
points: Follow the stone maker's water or lubrication instructions; not every water stone should be soaked.
The working surface should be flat enough and the support should not move.
Marker on the edge bevel shows where the abrasive is actually contacting and helps correct the angle.
content.takeaway: Stable stone, correct contact, complete edge coverage.

question.prompt: The stone holder moves during a sharpening pass. What should you do?

options.text: Stop and stabilize it before continuing.
Increase pressure so the blade holds the stone in place.
Move faster so the support has less time to shift.
Change to a finer grit without correcting the support.

question.explanation: A moving stone compromises both safety and angle control.

recovery_questions.prompt: What does the marker method verify?

options.text: The exact HRC value of the steel after tempering
The carbide chemistry of the alloy under the microscope
Where the stone contacts and removes material on the edge bevel
The tang construction hidden inside the knife handle

recovery_questions.explanation: Ink removal makes sharpening contact visible.

lessons.title: Use the burr as evidence, then remove it

content.lead: The burr proves that abrasion reached the apex; it is not the desired final edge.
points: Aim for the smallest detectable burr that is continuous from heel to tip.
Reduce pressure and alternate sides during deburring until no directional hook remains.
Final testing should combine visual or burr checks with controlled cuts; paper alone can be fooled by a fragile wire edge.
content.takeaway: A good edge is clean, stable and consistent along its full length.

question.prompt: What does a burr present only in the middle prove?

options.text: The entire edge is finished from heel to tip.
The sharpening angle is perfect along the full blade.
The stone is too fine for any further work.
Only the middle has reached the apex.

question.explanation: A continuous burr is needed as evidence of complete apex reach on that side.

recovery_questions.prompt: What should happen to pressure during deburring?

options.text: Reduce it progressively while alternating sides.
Increase it steadily until the burr becomes larger.
Remain at maximum pressure on one side only.
Stop contacting the edge bevel before the burr is removed.

recovery_questions.explanation: Light alternating passes weaken and remove the burr while stabilizing the apex.

questions.prompt: Why must hand position adapt near a curved tip?

options.text: To create the largest possible burr only at the tip
To preserve local bevel contact as the blade profile changes
To polish the blade face instead of working the edge
To keep the wrist fixed while the contact point moves away

questions.explanation: The hand follows the changing geometry to keep the intended contact.

questions.prompt: Why should paper not be the only final sharpness test?

options.text: Paper can never reveal a catch or rough section in an edge.
Paper always damages every properly sharpened kitchen knife.
A fragile wire edge can cut paper yet fail in food.
Paper works only on serrated knives and not on plain edges.

questions.explanation: Use multiple checks to distinguish a stable apex from a temporary wire edge.

levels.title: Intermediate
levels.purpose: Apply the same full-book themes through mechanisms, trade-offs and realistic use cases rather than simple recognition.

modules.title: Anatomy & Construction
modules.summary: Explain how parts, dimensions and construction choices interact instead of merely naming them.

lessons.title: Read anatomy as a system

content.lead: At intermediate level, naming parts is not enough: explain how dimensions and transitions change use.
points: Blade height affects knuckle clearance and guidance; spine thickness and distal taper affect stiffness and mass distribution.
Heel, belly and tip geometry determine where different cutting movements make contact.
A bolster transition and handle geometry change how the hand can move forward or backward on the knife.
content.takeaway: Use anatomy to explain behaviour, not just vocabulary.

question.prompt: A customer wants more knuckle clearance without a longer blade. Which feature is most directly relevant?

options.text: Higher chromium content
More heel height
More Damascus layers
A finer finishing stone

question.explanation: Knuckle clearance is primarily geometric, especially blade height near the working heel area.

recovery_questions.prompt: Two knives share the same length but one feels easier to redirect. Which anatomical factor can help explain it?

options.text: A higher nominal carbon percentage alone
A darker blade finish
A larger layer count
Less mass concentrated toward the tip

recovery_questions.explanation: Where mass sits along the blade changes rotational inertia and handling.

lessons.title: Separate construction facts from quality claims

content.lead: Intermediate product knowledge requires explaining what a construction feature proves and what it does not.
points: Full tang, hidden tang and through tang change structure and mass distribution, but none is automatically superior in every knife.
Forging, welding and stamping are process descriptions; execution quality and downstream grinding and heat treatment still matter.
Decorative blade-face features should not be confused with cross-section geometry or cutting performance.
content.takeaway: Ask what the feature changes mechanically before calling it better.

question.prompt: A hidden-tang knife and a full-tang knife both feel solid. What is the best comparison?

options.text: Declare the full tang superior without further inspection.
Compare only the visible handle material.
Compare dimensions, assembly, balance and intended loads.
Use layer count as the deciding construction metric.

question.explanation: Tang style is one structural input among several.

recovery_questions.prompt: What does a forged blade label fail to tell you by itself?

options.text: Whether metal deformation occurred during manufacture
Final grind and heat-treatment quality
Whether the blade began as a steel workpiece
Whether a shaping process was used

recovery_questions.explanation: Forging says something about process, not the quality of every later step.

questions.prompt: Why can a pronounced bolster transition matter ergonomically?

options.text: It can constrain forward grip positions.
It determines the alloy's carbide chemistry.
It fixes the HRC of the edge.
It proves the blade was powder-metallurgy steel.

questions.explanation: The handle-to-blade interface affects where fingers can settle.

questions.prompt: A hammered blade face releases food differently. What should be checked before attributing the effect to the hammering?

options.text: Only the printed steel grade
Only the tang construction
Only the sharpening stone grit
Overall geometry and contact pattern

questions.explanation: Blade-face features interact with the complete geometry and food contact.

modules.title: Steel Properties
modules.summary: Use trade-offs and microstructural reasoning to compare steels for real tasks.

lessons.title: Reason across the five steel dimensions

content.lead: Intermediate competence means identifying trade-offs between properties for a concrete use.
points: Higher hardness can improve resistance to rolling but may reduce misuse tolerance when geometry is very thin.
High wear resistance can preserve cutting character longer while making reprofiling slower.
Fine microstructure supports refined apex stability, while carbide-rich structures can favour long-lasting aggressive slicing bite.
content.takeaway: Match the compromise to the task rather than maximizing every number.

question.prompt: A user wants very thin geometry and occasionally twists the blade in dense food. Which concern rises most?

options.text: Lateral-load toughness
Logo durability
Handle colour stability
Layer-count visibility

question.explanation: Thin geometry plus lateral misuse raises fracture/chipping risk even in high-performing steel.

recovery_questions.prompt: A steel keeps a toothy slicing edge for a long time but reprofiles slowly. Which dimension is probably strong?

options.text: Handle ergonomics
Passivation speed only
Wear resistance
Tang visibility

recovery_questions.explanation: Strong abrasive wear resistance often trades against rapid material removal in sharpening.

lessons.title: Connect corrosion and sharpening to microstructure

content.lead: At intermediate level, explain why nominal composition does not map directly to use.
points: Chromium in solution supports passivation; chromium tied in carbides is less available for corrosion protection.
Sharpening speed depends on matrix hardness, carbide hardness/volume and abrasive choice, not just HRC.
Burr formation and removal can make a nominally softer steel less pleasant to sharpen than a harder fine-grained steel.
content.takeaway: Ask where the alloying elements and carbides ended up after heat treatment.

question.prompt: Two stainless steels contain similar chromium, but one pits more easily. Which explanation is plausible?

options.text: Different handle length alone
Different logo engraving depth
Different packaging humidity at sale only
Carbon balance and chromium availability

question.explanation: Nominal chromium does not show how much remains available for passivation.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why might diamond abrasive help on a carbide-rich wear-resistant steel?

options.text: It cuts very hard carbides efficiently.
It lowers the HRC before sharpening starts.
It dissolves chromium into the matrix.
It converts the edge into a convex grind automatically.

recovery_questions.explanation: Abrasive choice should suit the hardness of the particles being cut.

questions.prompt: Why can two steels at 60 HRC behave differently at the edge?

options.text: HRC controls only blade colour.
Different microstructure and carbide balance
One must secretly be softer than measured.
Same HRC guarantees identical wear and toughness.

questions.explanation: Hardness is one measured property, not a complete description of the steel.

questions.prompt: Which shortcut is least reliable?

options.text: Corrosion resistance can vary among stainless steels.
Burr behaviour affects sharpening feel.
Softer steel is always easier to sharpen.
Abrasive choice matters on hard carbides.

questions.explanation: Sharpening response is multi-factor, so hardness alone is an unreliable shortcut.

modules.title: Alloying, Heat Treatment & PM
modules.summary: Follow alloying elements through phases, carbides, heat treatment and powder-metallurgy processing.

lessons.title: Track carbon, chromium and carbides

content.lead: Intermediate metallurgy follows where atoms and phases go, not just percentages.
points: Carbon can remain dissolved in austenite/martensite or become part of separate carbide crystals.
Chromium tied in carbides cannot contribute fully to passivation at the same time.
Molybdenum, vanadium, tungsten, cobalt, nickel and nitrogen support different metallurgical roles; none is a universal quality badge.
content.takeaway: Ask what structure an element helps create and what trade-off follows.

question.prompt: Why can more carbon complicate corrosion resistance in a stainless steel?

options.text: It always removes molybdenum from the alloy entirely.
More chromium can be tied up in carbides.
It automatically lowers hardness below kitchen-knife levels.
It turns martensite directly into handle resin.

question.explanation: Carbon and chromium interact through carbide formation and solution balance.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is the main knife-steel role of vanadium at higher effective carbide volume?

options.text: Create the passive chromium oxide film by itself
Make every steel easy to polish on soft abrasives
Eliminate the need for tempering after quenching
Form very hard carbides that raise abrasive wear resistance

recovery_questions.explanation: Vanadium carbides are extremely hard and strongly affect wear and abrasive choice.

lessons.title: Connect heat treatment to final microstructure

content.lead: Intermediate understanding links austenitizing, quenching, sub-zero treatment and tempering to the finished edge.
points: Austenitizing dissolves selected carbon/alloy into high-temperature austenite and sets up the hardening transformation.
Quenching creates martensite; retained austenite can remain if transformation is incomplete.
Powder metallurgy improves starting uniformity for highly alloyed steels, but heat treatment still determines the final phase and carbide balance.
content.takeaway: PM steel is not finished performance until heat treatment and grinding are right.

question.prompt: Why might a deep-freeze step follow quenching in a demanding steel?

options.text: To add new carbon atoms from the surrounding air
To create a Damascus pattern on the blade surface
To reduce retained austenite and continue the intended transformation
To soften the handle before final assembly

question.explanation: Sub-zero processing can push more retained austenite toward the desired hardened structure.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why does powder metallurgy not remove the need for good heat treatment?

options.text: PM changes only the colour of the steel powder.
Heat treatment still sets final phases and hardness.
Heat treatment is needed only for conventional steels.
Powder steels cannot form martensite without surface coating.

recovery_questions.explanation: Processing route and heat treatment solve different parts of the metallurgy problem.

mini_test.title: Applied check · Alloying, Heat Treatment & PM

questions.prompt: Which statement about cobalt is best?

options.text: It can support demanding heat-treatment stability in suitable alloys.
Its presence automatically makes any blade tougher.
It is the main element that creates stainless passivation.
It guarantees fine carbides regardless of processing route.

questions.explanation: Cobalt has a specific metallurgical role, not a universal prestige effect.

questions.prompt: What is a reasonable reason to use vacuum heat treatment?

options.text: Guarantee a single-bevel edge without grinding
Replace tempering with a decorative process
Increase handle moisture resistance
Atmosphere control during high-temperature treatment

questions.explanation: Atmosphere control helps protect the steel during demanding high-temperature stages.

modules.title: Xinzuo Materials
modules.summary: Compare blade steels and handle materials against explicit user priorities and design effects.

lessons.title: Compare Xinzuo steels by use case

content.lead: Intermediate staff should compare steels by design direction, not recite a prestige ladder.
points: ZDP-189 prioritizes very high hardness and edge life; M390 emphasizes wear and corrosion resistance; SRS13 pursues another premium balance.
10Cr15CoMoV and newer all-round stainless choices target broad kitchen use with different balances.
Blue Steel No. 2, 14C28N, 440C and 1.4116 illustrate how different users can rationally prefer different maintenance, toughness and sharpening profiles.
content.takeaway: A steel recommendation should be conditional: good for whom, doing what, with what maintenance tolerance?

question.prompt: A user prioritizes corrosion resistance and long wear life over easy reprofiling. Which direction fits best?

options.text: A premium wear- and corrosion-oriented stainless such as M390
A reactive carbon steel chosen mainly for easy water-stone response
A moderate soft stainless chosen mainly for forgiving deformation
Any steel solely because it has the highest listed layer count

question.explanation: The requested priorities align with wear/corrosion emphasis, accepting a sharpening trade-off.

recovery_questions.prompt: A skilled sharpener wants responsive water-stone feedback and accepts reactive care. Which direction is plausible?

options.text: Only the highest-chromium powder steel
Any 1.4116 blade regardless of heat treatment
Blue Steel No. 2
The steel with the most decorative layers

recovery_questions.explanation: Blue Steel No. 2 is a deliberate carbon-steel choice when sharpening response and care habits fit.

lessons.title: Use handle material as a design variable

content.lead: Intermediate evaluation connects material properties to mass, moisture, surface feel and maintenance.
points: G10 and technical composites can provide stable moisture-resistant structures; natural woods offer distinct feel and density but need appropriate care.
Stabilized wood and pakka wood deliberately modify natural material with resin for greater stability.
Material density can alter rearward mass and perceived balance, so the same blade can feel different with another handle build.
content.takeaway: Handle material should support the ergonomic and environmental brief.

question.prompt: A wet professional environment and low-maintenance priority favour which handle logic?

options.text: Choose untreated wood solely because it looks more traditional.
Choose the densest material regardless of hand fit.
Ignore surface texture because material name determines grip.
Prefer stable moisture-resistant technical materials, then confirm ergonomics.

question.explanation: Environment and care tolerance matter, but fit still has to be tested.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can stabilized wood behave differently from untreated wood?

options.text: Resin impregnation changes moisture response and structural stability.
It changes the blade steel into a stainless alloy.
It forces a different edge angle during sharpening.
It removes all mass from the rear of the knife.

recovery_questions.explanation: Stabilization intentionally changes the properties of the wood/resin composite.

questions.prompt: Why is 'equivalent to VG10' not the same as 'identical to VG10'?

options.text: Equivalent means the steels share the same exact heat-treatment history.
Nominally similar performance/composition does not erase specification and process differences.
Equivalent means every carbide is identical in size and chemistry.
Equivalent means the brand names are legally interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Similarity does not prove identity of composition, processing or final microstructure.

questions.prompt: A heavier handle makes a knife feel more neutral in a forward grip. What changed?

options.text: The blade's chemical composition
The number of bevels at the edge
Mass distribution around the working grip
The corrosion threshold of the steel

questions.explanation: Handle mass influences balance without changing blade metallurgy.

modules.title: Damascus & Layered Construction
modules.summary: Evaluate Damascus claims through construction, metallurgy, geometry and realistic wear mechanisms.

lessons.title: Evaluate Damascus construction in sequence

content.lead: Intermediate knowledge separates construction, pattern formation, layer count and edge geometry before discussing performance.
points: Pattern-welded cladding, full-Damascus construction and surface-decorated monosteel are different categories.
Layer count describes how a billet or construction is assembled, not the sharpness of the apex.
Historical crucible Damascus and Chinese bintie traditions are historically distinct from modern pattern welding.
content.takeaway: Ask: what construction, what steels, what edge geometry, what heat treatment?

question.prompt: A blade shows a complex pattern and 67 layers. What still must be established before judging cutting performance?

options.text: Only whether the pattern is visually symmetrical
Core/edge material, geometry and heat treatment
Only the retail price of the series
Only the number of handle pins

question.explanation: Layer count does not replace information about the working edge and its processing.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why should modern pattern-welded Damascus not be presented as identical to historical crucible Damascus?

options.text: Historical Damascus had no carbon at all.
Modern Damascus is always only laser decoration.
Crucible steel cannot form any visible pattern.
They use different metallurgical routes.

recovery_questions.explanation: Similar visual language can come from different historical and metallurgical processes.

lessons.title: Explain differential wear without exaggeration

content.lead: Intermediate explanation distinguishes microscopic edge texture from geometric resharpening.
points: Different layers can abrade at different rates and create micro-serration-like texture at the apex.
This can sustain slicing bite, but the apex still rounds, deforms and eventually needs maintenance.
Use changes how the effect develops; board contact, food and sharpening alter the edge over time.
content.takeaway: Describe the mechanism and its limits in the same sentence.

question.prompt: Which claim is technically safest for differential wear?

options.text: It recreates the original factory edge angle continuously.
It makes future sharpening unnecessary for the life of the knife.
It may preserve slicing bite while normal edge wear still continues.
It guarantees identical behaviour in every food and board condition.

question.explanation: The effect is real but limited: texture can persist while overall sharpness still declines.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can slicing bite remain useful after peak push-cut sharpness declines?

options.text: The handle becomes heavier and pushes the blade forward.
Microtexture still supports sliding bite.
The steel automatically raises its HRC during use.
The urasuki deepens itself with every board contact.

recovery_questions.explanation: Slicing bite and peak apex refinement are related but distinct.

questions.prompt: What is the first check when a product is described as Damascus?

options.text: Structural layering or surface decoration?
Assume the edge is harder than every monosteel.
Assume more layers mean lower cutting resistance.
Assume the blade uses a single-bevel geometry.

questions.explanation: Construction category must be established before performance claims.

questions.prompt: Which observation would weaken a 'self-sharpening' marketing claim?

options.text: The edge shows useful slicing texture during wear.
Different layers can abrade at different rates.
Use pattern can influence edge development.
It still needs normal sharpening.

questions.explanation: A mechanism that changes wear behaviour is not the same as perpetual sharpening.

modules.title: Geometry & Bevels
modules.summary: Connect cross-section, edge support, asymmetry and specialist reference surfaces to cutting and maintenance.

lessons.title: Connect cross-section to cutting behaviour

content.lead: Intermediate geometry asks how edge support, thickness and face shape change resistance and food separation.
points: Convex, flat and hollow sections distribute material differently behind the edge.
A low edge angle can reduce cutting resistance but needs enough steel/toughness behind it for the intended load.
Food release depends on face geometry and contact, not simply on edge sharpness.
content.takeaway: Edge angle, thickness behind the edge and face geometry must be read together.

question.prompt: Two equally sharp knives cut a carrot differently. One wedges badly. What is the most relevant next check?

options.text: Geometry behind the edge
Handle colour and packaging
Only the HRC number
Only the layer count

question.explanation: Wedging is strongly influenced by the geometry supporting the apex.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a hollow grind feel low in cutting resistance but less supported?

options.text: It increases handle mass behind the grip.
It raises chromium in solution during cutting.
It removes support behind the edge.
It automatically creates a full tang.

recovery_questions.explanation: Cross-section determines how much steel supports the edge.

lessons.title: Preserve asymmetry and specialist reference surfaces

content.lead: Intermediate sharpening advice must preserve the designed asymmetry rather than normalize every edge to 50/50.
points: Mildly asymmetric double bevels can steer slightly and should retain their intended ratio through maintenance.
On urasuki knives the reverse reference lands must stay flat/lightly worked; raising the reverse creates the wrong geometry.
Single-bevel handedness matters because orientation changes the working geometry relative to the cut.
content.takeaway: Maintenance should conserve the geometry that makes the knife behave as designed.

question.prompt: A 70/30 double bevel is sharpened with equal work on both sides for many cycles. What risk arises?

options.text: The steel becomes non-stainless.
The tang changes from hidden to full.
The handle gains front mass.
The intended asymmetry can gradually be erased.

question.explanation: Sharpening alters geometry over time, so stroke symmetry is not always the target.

recovery_questions.prompt: What happens if the flat reverse of an urasuki knife is repeatedly sharpened at a normal edge angle?

options.text: Reference lands and specialist geometry degrade.
The urasuki becomes deeper and more correct.
The knife becomes a powder-metallurgy steel.
The handle balance automatically shifts forward.

recovery_questions.explanation: The reverse is a reference system, not a second normal bevel.

questions.prompt: Which pair most directly controls edge support?

options.text: Logo size and blade finish
Edge angle plus behind-edge thickness
Handle colour and layer pattern
Packaging weight and steel name

questions.explanation: Support is geometric and material, not decorative.

questions.prompt: Why should handedness be verified on a specialist single-bevel model?

options.text: Only left-handed knives can hold a burr.
Right-handed knives always use softer steel.
Orientation changes steering and working-face behaviour.
Handedness determines chromium content.

questions.explanation: Strong asymmetric geometry interacts with the direction of use.

modules.title: Knife Families & Ergonomics
modules.summary: Choose by movement, load path, mass distribution and real grip rather than by name alone.

lessons.title: Map knife families to movement and load

content.lead: Intermediate selection links blade family to motion, contact length, flexibility and load direction.
points: Flat/tall board knives favour direct or advancing board work; long narrow slicers exploit draw length.
Boning knives favour manoeuvrability around joints; fillet knives may use designed flexibility; deba uses a robust specialist fish-butchery geometry.
Bone choppers and frozen-food tools need geometry designed for impact/hard material rather than repurposed thin general-purpose edges.
content.takeaway: Choose by movement and load path, not silhouette alone.

question.prompt: A cook mostly makes long clean portions of boneless roast. Which geometry solves the task first?

options.text: A short thick bone chopper for vertical impact
A long slicer for drawing strokes
A highly flexible paring knife for in-hand work
A broad cleaver chosen mainly for food transfer

question.explanation: The primary problem is long clean slicing, so edge length and draw geometry come first.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is a deba not a universal bone chopper?

options.text: It is always flexible like a fillet knife.
It cannot contact any fish bone at all.
It is designed mainly for bread crusts.
It is specialized for controlled fish butchery.

recovery_questions.explanation: Specialist robustness has a defined job and does not imply unlimited load tolerance.

lessons.title: Reason about balance and rotational inertia

content.lead: Intermediate ergonomics explains why equal-weight knives can move differently.
points: Mass farther from the grip raises rotational inertia more than the same mass near the hand.
Blade-forward balance can feel stable in push/down strokes but asks more effort to stop or redirect.
Grip position changes lever arms, so balance must be tested in the customer's normal hold.
content.takeaway: Total weight is not enough; where the weight sits matters.

question.prompt: Two 200 g knives differ mainly because one carries more mass near the tip. What should you expect?

options.text: Identical handling because total mass is equal
Lower corrosion resistance in the tip-heavy knife
More rotational resistance from tip-heavy mass
A lower HRC caused by forward mass distribution

question.explanation: Rotational inertia depends on mass distribution as well as total mass.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can a long handle improve balance for a forward pinch-grip user?

options.text: Long handles always reduce blade thickness.
Rearward mass counterbalances blade mass
Long handles increase chromium available for passivation.
Long handles force all users into the same grip.

recovery_questions.explanation: A handle can act as a counterweight; fit still depends on the actual user.

questions.prompt: Which factor best distinguishes a boning knife from a bone chopper?

options.text: Manoeuvrability versus impact tolerance
Whether the handle has three rivets or two
Whether the blade is polished or satin
Whether the logo is etched or printed

questions.explanation: The mechanical task, not cosmetic construction details, defines the family.

questions.prompt: What should happen after functionally suitable knives are identified?

options.text: Choose the highest HRC without handling the knives.
Choose the most expensive Damascus pattern.
Ignore ergonomics and compare packaging only.
Compare grip, weight and balance in hand.

questions.explanation: Once function is solved, ergonomic fit becomes the next selection filter.

modules.title: Cutting Techniques
modules.summary: Diagnose mismatches between movement, edge profile and load, and respect specialist technique boundaries.

lessons.title: Diagnose movement–geometry mismatch

content.lead: Intermediate technique diagnoses why a movement is inefficient instead of simply naming it.
points: A flat edge used in a wide rock may leave uncut sections; a highly curved edge used in pure vertical chopping may not contact the board fully.
Push cutting adds slicing travel and can reduce splitting in dense vegetables compared with pure pressing.
Draw slicing uses edge length and reduces compression on delicate foods.
content.takeaway: When a technique feels forced, inspect the path and blade profile before adding force.

question.prompt: A carrot cracks before a sharp gyuto completes the cut. What is a useful first correction?

options.text: Add controlled forward travel.
Increase vertical force while keeping the edge stationary.
Twist the blade sideways to open the crack.
Move the supporting fingers into the cutting path.

question.explanation: A slicing component can reduce wedging/splitting by moving the edge through the food.

recovery_questions.prompt: A curved chef's knife leaves the heel above the board during a direct chop. What does that suggest?

options.text: The steel has insufficient chromium.
The handle is too moisture resistant.
The path mismatches the edge curve.
The tang is too visible.

recovery_questions.explanation: Board contact reveals whether movement and edge profile match.

lessons.title: Choose specialist technique boundaries

content.lead: Intermediate users distinguish controlled specialist work from misuse that merely looks forceful.
points: Bone/joint work follows anatomical gaps and uses an appropriate blade rather than levering a fine edge.
Filleting combines contour following with only the flexibility engineered into the blade.
Crushing, transferring and scraping should use appropriate blade faces/spines or dedicated tools without dragging the cutting edge sideways.
content.takeaway: A technique is correct only when the blade geometry and load direction support it.

question.prompt: A cook scrapes chopped food sideways with the cutting edge. What is the better practice?

options.text: Press harder so the edge stays flat on the board.
Increase the edge angle before every scrape.
Use a glass board so the food moves more easily.
Use the spine, face or a scraper.

question.explanation: Sideways scraping loads and abrades the apex in a direction it is not designed for.

recovery_questions.prompt: A narrow boning knife reaches a hard joint. What should the user seek?

options.text: The anatomical path around the joint rather than brute force through it
The point where maximum lateral twist opens the joint
The hardest spot to strike repeatedly with the spine
A way to hold the food in the air during the cut

recovery_questions.explanation: Specialist knives solve geometry problems; they are not substitutes for controlled anatomy-aware work.

questions.prompt: Why can a draw cut improve the surface of delicate fish?

options.text: It increases lateral levering at the cut face.
It reduces compression by using more edge.
It keeps the edge stationary while the food moves.
It makes blade thickness irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Long slicing uses edge travel to cut cleanly with less compression.

questions.prompt: What makes an in-hand peeling technique higher risk?

options.text: The blade always contains less chromium.
The handle always becomes blade-heavy.
Edge path close to hand/body
The edge always becomes convex during use.

questions.explanation: Proximity to the body raises the need for control and appropriate small-tool technique.

modules.title: Safe Use & Handling
modules.summary: Diagnose interacting risk factors and design predictable handling from setup through transport and storage.

lessons.title: Diagnose the chain that creates risk

content.lead: Intermediate safety identifies interacting causes before an incident, not just isolated rules.
points: Unstable board + unstable food + excessive force compound one another; fixing only one may leave the cut unpredictable.
A dull or damaged edge can increase required force, but a sharp edge still requires controlled path and hand placement.
Knife choice is part of safety because geometry determines whether a task encourages correct load directions.
content.takeaway: Treat an unexpected need for force as diagnostic information.

question.prompt: A sharp knife suddenly needs much more force in a familiar cut. What should happen first?

options.text: Increase force until the cut behaves normally again.
Stop and diagnose edge, stability, tool and path.
Move the supporting hand closer to guide the blade.
Add sideways twist to reduce resistance.

question.explanation: Unexpected resistance should trigger diagnosis, not automatic compensation with force.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can the wrong knife increase safety risk even if it is sharp?

options.text: Sharp steel cannot be used safely on any food.
A wrong knife always has lower HRC.
A wrong knife always has a hidden tang.
Its geometry can encourage unsafe load directions.

recovery_questions.explanation: Tool fit is part of safe load management.

lessons.title: Design safe handling beyond the workstation

content.lead: Intermediate handling considers visibility, communication, transport and storage as one control system.
points: Passing requires deliberate orientation and confirmation; moving through a kitchen requires a low, still, predictable blade path.
Transport beyond the workstation should use suitable guards, rolls or cases rather than improvised wrapping.
Storage protects both people and the apex by preventing hidden hand contact and hard-object impacts.
content.takeaway: Visibility plus predictable orientation are the core controls when the knife is not cutting.

question.prompt: Why is a knife loose in a utensil drawer a double problem?

options.text: It reduces the chromium content and changes the steel grade.
It makes the tang shorter and the handle heavier.
Hand-injury risk plus hard-contact edge damage
It automatically creates a convex bevel.

question.explanation: Safe storage protects both user and edge condition.

recovery_questions.prompt: What is the best transport choice outside the workstation?

options.text: A loose towel with the edge orientation unknown
A fitted guard, roll or case
A bare knife inside a general bag with utensils
Holding the knife upright by the blade face

recovery_questions.explanation: Transport systems should secure the blade and make its position predictable.

questions.prompt: Which correction addresses the greatest number of risk factors at once?

options.text: Pause, stabilize setup and choose a suitable cutting path/tool.
Grip the knife harder and keep the same setup.
Increase speed before the ingredient can move.
Move the board closer to the counter edge.

questions.explanation: Good safety corrections remove instability rather than masking it.

questions.prompt: Why is passing the handle first safer?

options.text: It makes the blade steel softer during transfer.
It increases balance toward the handle permanently.
It prevents all possible injuries regardless of communication.
Controlled grip with the edge oriented away

questions.explanation: Orientation and communication work together; handle-first improves the transfer geometry.

modules.title: Care & Cutting Boards
modules.summary: Compare board systems and diagnose maintenance operations by the actual failure mode.

lessons.title: Compare board materials as systems

content.lead: Intermediate board choice balances edge wear, stability, hygiene, maintenance and environmental trade-offs.
points: End-grain wood is edge-friendly but needs wood-appropriate care; plastic is hygienically practical but can scar and raises microplastic concerns.
Bamboo can be usable but is often harder than preferred for very fine edges; resilient rubber/professional synthetics can be very edge-friendly.
Wood-fibre resin composites are stable and durable but generally harder and less yielding than traditional wood.
content.takeaway: There is no universal board winner; choose against the knife and environment.

question.prompt: A user wants maximum edge friendliness for a very thin hard edge and accepts maintenance. Which direction is strongest?

options.text: A suitable yielding wood or resilient professional board
A polished glass board for easy cleaning
A stone slab because it cannot groove
A metal plate because it is dimensionally stable

question.explanation: Fine hard edges benefit from surfaces that yield rather than concentrate impact.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why might a resin-bonded fibre board be chosen despite being harder than wood?

options.text: It always improves edge retention compared with end grain.
It is chemically identical to natural wood.
Its thinness, stability and durability may suit the environment.
It makes knife cleaning unnecessary.

recovery_questions.explanation: Board choice is a trade-off, not a one-property ranking.

lessons.title: Diagnose maintenance needs by failure mode

content.lead: Intermediate maintenance distinguishes corrosion, edge deformation, dulling and handle deterioration instead of applying one remedy to all.
points: Stable patina on carbon steel is not the same as active rust; stainless pitting indicates localized corrosion that still needs attention.
A honing rod can realign some rolled edges but cannot recreate a worn or chipped apex that needs abrasive removal.
Natural wood handles, composites and technical polymers fail in different ways and need material-appropriate care.
content.takeaway: Identify the failure mode before choosing the maintenance operation.

question.prompt: A blade has active orange rust spots. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: This is always a harmless sign of good carbon steel.
This proves the blade has become tougher.
This is a normal sharpening burr on the blade face.
This is corrosion to address, not a desirable stable patina.

question.explanation: Active rust and stable patina have different appearance and maintenance meaning.

recovery_questions.prompt: A rolled edge improves after light honing. What likely happened?

options.text: The edge was partly realigned.
The steel's carbide volume increased.
The blade became a higher HRC grade.
The tang was straightened inside the handle.

recovery_questions.explanation: Honing can realign certain deformations; it is not the same as grinding a new apex.

questions.prompt: What concern belongs specifically to plastic boards in the book's comparison?

options.text: They are always harder than glass
Surface scarring and a real microplastic trade-off
They cannot be sanitized at all
They always absorb more water than end-grain wood

questions.explanation: Plastic has practical hygiene advantages but also wear/scarring and microplastic trade-offs.

questions.prompt: When should a natural wood handle receive different care from G10?

options.text: Only when the blade is single bevel.
Only when the steel exceeds 60 HRC.
When wood reacts differently to moisture
Only when the knife has Damascus cladding.

questions.explanation: Handle care follows the material's own moisture and surface behaviour.

modules.title: Sharpening & Edge Maintenance
modules.summary: Use contact, burr, local correction and abrasive choice as evidence-driven controls.

lessons.title: Sharpen from evidence, not stroke counts

content.lead: Intermediate sharpening uses marker, scratch feel, burr location and local edge condition to decide where more work is needed.
points: A fixed pass count is unreliable because steel, abrasive, pressure, angle and starting condition vary.
A burr proves apex contact only where it exists; local deficits should be corrected without overgrinding finished areas.
Pressure should fall as the apex is refined; a finer stone is useful only when it serves the desired finish or edge behaviour.
content.takeaway: Use evidence to decide the next stroke.

question.prompt: The middle has a burr but the heel does not. What is the best next step?

options.text: Continue heavy passes everywhere until the middle burr doubles.
Work the heel locally, then return to balanced complete passes.
Ignore the heel because a middle burr proves the full edge is done.
Raise the angle only at the middle to compensate.

question.explanation: Correct local deficits without unnecessarily removing steel from completed zones.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is counting ten passes per side a weak rule?

options.text: Every pass removes exactly the same amount of steel.
Ten passes always create a complete burr.
Pass counts determine the steel's heat treatment.
Abrasion needs vary with steel, stone and edge.

recovery_questions.explanation: Sharpening progress must be observed, not assumed from a fixed count.

lessons.title: Control burr and choose abrasives intelligently

content.lead: Intermediate sharpening separates burr creation, apex refinement and abrasive selection.
points: A large burr wastes steel and can fold into a wire edge that falsely appears sharp.
Alternating light passes weaken the burr and centre the apex; stropping may help but should not rescue poor stone work.
High-carbide steels may benefit from harder/faster abrasives; abrasive choice should match the particles being cut.
content.takeaway: Create only enough burr to prove contact, then remove it cleanly.

question.prompt: A knife slices paper once but quickly loses bite in food. What sharpening defect is plausible?

options.text: The tang is too short.
The handle is too moisture resistant.
A fragile wire edge remains at the apex.
The steel contains too much nickel for any edge.
