question.explanation: A wire edge can pass a paper test briefly without being a stable apex.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why might a conventional soft abrasive feel slow on a high-vanadium steel?

options.text: Vanadium lowers the handle's friction.
Hard vanadium carbides resist the abrasive.
Vanadium prevents all burr formation.
Vanadium makes the blade permanently convex.

recovery_questions.explanation: Abrasive hardness and efficiency matter when hard carbides dominate wear resistance.

questions.prompt: The marker disappears only at the apex, leaving most of the edge bevel inked. What does that suggest?

options.text: The sharpening angle may be too high.
The stone is necessarily too coarse.
The steel is necessarily too soft.
The burr has already been fully removed.

questions.explanation: Contact only at the apex indicates a steeper angle than the existing bevel.

questions.prompt: What is the role of stropping in a sound basic process?

options.text: A mandatory replacement for correct bevel contact
A way to create the primary grind from scratch
A method to raise the steel's HRC after sharpening
Optional help after sound stone work

questions.explanation: The stone should already leave a clean, stable edge; stropping is supplementary.

levels.title: Advanced
levels.purpose: Diagnose interacting causes, resolve ambiguous trade-offs and defend recommendations with evidence across the same full-book themes.

modules.title: Anatomy & Construction
modules.summary: Infer behaviour from combined geometry and construction while avoiding unsupported quality claims.

lessons.title: Infer behaviour without overclaiming

content.lead: Advanced analysis combines anatomy, geometry and mass while keeping causal claims narrow.
points: A thin spine does not prove a thin edge; distal taper does not prove low cutting resistance near the heel.
Blade height, belly curve, tip mass and bolster transition can jointly change technique and fatigue.
Visible construction should be treated as evidence about structure, not as a substitute for measurements of working geometry.
content.takeaway: State what a feature supports, then state what still needs measurement.

question.prompt: A knife has a thin distal tip but feels wedge-like in carrots near the heel. Which explanation is strongest?

options.text: Distal taper guarantees low resistance everywhere, so the food is at fault.
The handle material must be causing the wedging.
Heel-area thickness and face geometry
The knife must have lost corrosion resistance near the heel.

question.explanation: Geometry is local; a feature at the tip does not define the whole blade cross-section.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which claim best respects the limits of anatomy alone?

options.text: Tall blade helps clearance; comfort still depends on grip.
A tall blade is always more ergonomic for every hand.
A full tang proves superior edge retention.
A forged bolster proves a finer apex.

recovery_questions.explanation: Advanced explanation distinguishes plausible contribution from universal conclusion.

lessons.title: Diagnose construction claims from incomplete evidence

content.lead: Advanced staff should resist common sales inferences that jump from one construction feature to global quality.
points: A welded bolster can be excellent or poor depending on joint quality, heat control, grinding and finishing.
A hidden tang can be durable when dimensions, materials and assembly suit the load; a full tang can still be poorly executed.
Forging may alter shape and grain flow, but finished performance remains dominated by the complete metallurgy and geometry.
content.takeaway: Advanced product claims require several independent pieces of evidence.

question.prompt: A competitor claims 'welded bolster = cheap knife'. What is the best technical response?

options.text: All welded bolsters are superior to forged ones.
Welding method alone does not establish overall quality.
Bolster construction has no structural relevance at all.
Only blade HRC is needed to settle the question.

question.explanation: The correct response evaluates execution rather than accepting a categorical shortcut.

recovery_questions.prompt: A hidden-tang knife fails at the handle after heavy lateral abuse. What can you conclude about hidden tangs generally?

options.text: Hidden tang construction is universally unsafe.
Full tang knives cannot fail under lateral abuse.
Very little without separating design, assembly and misuse.
The blade steel caused the handle failure by definition.

recovery_questions.explanation: One failure under abnormal load does not establish a universal hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Two knives share blade height and weight, yet one feels slower to turn. What additional measurement is most useful?

options.text: Nominal chromium percentage alone
Packaging dimensions
Number of visible rivets
Grip-relative mass distribution

questions.explanation: Rotational handling depends strongly on mass distribution, not just total weight.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a construction-quality claim?

options.text: Fit, joints, dimensions and load performance
A single label such as forged or full tang
The highest visible layer count
The most expensive handle species

questions.explanation: Advanced assessment uses multiple structural and performance observations.

modules.title: Steel Properties
modules.summary: Resolve multi-variable steel choices and diagnose behaviour from hardness, matrix and carbide structure.

lessons.title: Select steel from a multi-variable brief

content.lead: Advanced steel selection resolves competing priorities instead of looking for a universal optimum.
points: A professional prep cook may value corrosion stability, predictable sharpening and toughness differently from an enthusiast chasing maximum wear resistance.
Very thin edge geometry magnifies the consequences of toughness and misuse tolerance.
Maintenance skill and abrasive access are legitimate design inputs because they change the practical cost of high wear resistance.
content.takeaway: The best steel is the best compromise for the whole operating context.

question.prompt: A busy cook cuts acidic food all day, wants thin geometry, and uses ordinary water stones. Which priority set is most coherent?

options.text: Maximum carbide volume regardless of sharpening or chipping tolerance
Reactive carbon behaviour with no concern for immediate drying
Highest HRC available regardless of edge geometry
Strong corrosion resistance, adequate toughness and manageable sharpening response

question.explanation: The brief contains corrosion, geometry and sharpening constraints that must all be respected.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why might an enthusiast rationally choose a harder, more wear-resistant steel despite slower sharpening?

options.text: Harder steel always has greater toughness.
Long edge life may justify slower sharpening.
Wear resistance removes the need for edge geometry.
Slow sharpening guarantees better corrosion resistance.

recovery_questions.explanation: User capability and maintenance tools change which trade-off is acceptable.

lessons.title: Diagnose behaviour from hardness, carbides and matrix

content.lead: Advanced reasoning explains why nominally similar steels diverge after heat treatment.
points: Matrix hardness, carbide type/volume/size and retained phases jointly affect wear, toughness and sharpening response.
A very fine microstructure can support a clean apex even at high hardness; coarse or abundant carbides can change refinement and fracture behaviour.
Corrosion behaviour depends on alloying in solution as well as nominal composition and surface condition.
content.takeaway: Use HRC as one measurement inside a microstructural explanation.

question.prompt: Two samples of the same steel grade sharpen very differently. Which explanation is strongest?

options.text: Different heat treatment can change matrix, carbides and burr behaviour.
The steel name guarantees identical microstructure, so the report is impossible.
Only handle material can explain sharpening differences.
Layer count determines sharpening response even in monosteel.

question.explanation: Same nominal grade does not guarantee identical final microstructure.

recovery_questions.prompt: A steel shows excellent wear life but chips at a thin edge in misuse. Which two dimensions are in tension?

options.text: Corrosion resistance and handle weight
Blade length and sharpening angle
Tang type and board hygiene
Wear resistance and toughness/misuse tolerance

recovery_questions.explanation: High wear capability does not remove the need for adequate toughness at the chosen geometry.

questions.prompt: Which variable most strongly argues against maximizing hardness alone on a very thin knife?

options.text: Logo position
Box material
Misuse tolerance
Number of handle pins

questions.explanation: Very thin geometry can make misuse tolerance a limiting requirement.

questions.prompt: What would most strengthen a claim that one heat treatment is better?

options.text: A higher tempering temperature by itself
Use-specific performance evidence
A darker blade finish after treatment
A more complex steel name

questions.explanation: Advanced comparison needs outcome evidence, not a single process number.

modules.title: Alloying, Heat Treatment & PM
modules.summary: Diagnose heat-treatment outcomes and explain the real benefits and limits of powder metallurgy.

lessons.title: Reason through heat-treatment outcomes

content.lead: Advanced metallurgy traces a performance symptom back through phase balance and process choices.
points: Too little dissolution during austenitizing can limit hardness/available alloy; too much can enlarge grains or dissolve excessive carbides.
Quench severity and retained austenite affect final hardness and dimensional stability; sub-zero treatment can shift that balance.
Tempering trades as-quenched hardness/stress for usable stability and toughness, and can also modify carbide precipitation.
content.takeaway: Heat treatment is a sequence of linked decisions; no step can be judged in isolation.

question.prompt: A very hard blade shows unstable behaviour and unusually high retained austenite. Which process area deserves attention?

options.text: Handle polishing sequence
Packaging humidity only
Hardening transformation sequence
Number of Damascus layers

question.explanation: Retained austenite is directly tied to the hardening transformation sequence.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can an excessively aggressive austenitizing schedule hurt toughness?

options.text: It can coarsen grains or upset carbide balance.
It always reduces carbon to zero.
It converts the handle into martensite.
It eliminates every alloying element from the steel.

recovery_questions.explanation: Temperature/time choices influence grain size and dissolved alloy, which affect final behaviour.

lessons.title: Use powder metallurgy without treating it as magic

content.lead: Advanced reasoning recognizes what PM improves and what it cannot guarantee.
points: Rapid solidification of small droplets reduces segregation and can produce finer, more uniform carbide distributions in heavily alloyed steels.
PM allows alloy designs that would be difficult to process conventionally, but composition can still create high carbide volume and sharpening demands.
Final performance still depends on consolidation quality, heat treatment, grinding, edge geometry and intended use.
content.takeaway: PM improves material homogeneity; it does not erase alloy trade-offs.

question.prompt: Why can a PM steel still be difficult to sharpen?

options.text: PM prevents all abrasives from contacting the steel matrix.
High volume of very hard carbides
PM always raises hardness above every conventional steel.
PM replaces carbon with ceramic powder.

question.explanation: Fine distribution and low sharpening resistance are not the same property.

recovery_questions.prompt: What comparison best demonstrates a real PM advantage?

options.text: Higher retail price regardless of microstructure
More decorative layers on the blade face
More uniform microstructure at high alloy content
Longer handle on the finished knife

recovery_questions.explanation: PM's core metallurgical benefit is control of solidification and segregation.

mini_test.title: Diagnostic check · Alloying, Heat Treatment & PM

questions.prompt: What is the best reason to compare heat-treatment recipes by final performance rather than peak hardness?

options.text: HRC is unrelated to steel hardness.
Tempering cannot change any property after quenching.
Carbides have no influence on edge behaviour.
Balanced final microstructure

questions.explanation: Peak hardness can sacrifice other properties that the intended knife needs.

questions.prompt: Which statement about PM is too strong?

options.text: Every PM steel is universally superior.
PM can improve carbide distribution in highly alloyed steels.
PM does not replace good heat treatment.
Final geometry still affects cutting performance.

questions.explanation: PM is a processing advantage, not a universal performance guarantee.

modules.title: Xinzuo Materials
modules.summary: Build defensible steel and handle recommendations from explicit constraints, not prestige ladders.

lessons.title: Build a defensible Xinzuo steel shortlist

content.lead: Advanced staff should translate customer constraints into a shortlist and explain why excluded steels are less suitable.
points: ZDP-189 is compelling for maximum hardness/edge life but asks disciplined use and sharpening; M390 favours wear/corrosion; SRS13 targets another premium compromise.
14Cr14MoVNb represents Xinzuo's proprietary PM direction; 10Cr15CoMoV and 12Cr18MoV occupy broad stainless-use positions with different balances.
14C28N emphasizes fine structure/edge stability, while 440C and 1.4116 can serve more forgiving or conventional use cases.
content.takeaway: Recommend from the constraint set, then explain the rejected alternatives.

question.prompt: A careful enthusiast wants maximum edge life, owns diamond abrasives, and accepts low misuse tolerance. Which direction becomes more reasonable?

options.text: A moderate forgiving steel chosen specifically to avoid high hardness
Any reactive carbon steel solely because it rusts faster
The steel with the lowest wear resistance available
A very hard premium steel such as ZDP-189

question.explanation: The user's technique and abrasive access reduce the practical cost of the high-hardness trade-off.

recovery_questions.prompt: A restaurant wants easy care, high corrosion stability and predictable maintenance across many users. Which criterion should dominate over prestige?

options.text: Maximum nominal HRC regardless of users
Operational robustness and maintenance fit
Most expensive alloy in the catalogue
Highest visible layer count

recovery_questions.explanation: Shared professional use rewards predictable maintenance and tolerance more than abstract maximums.

lessons.title: Solve handle material, balance and environment together

content.lead: Advanced handle selection treats material as one variable in an ergonomic and environmental system.
points: Density changes mass distribution; surface texture changes security; moisture response changes maintenance; contour changes finger/wrist posture.
A premium natural wood can be the wrong choice in a wet high-turnover environment, while a technical composite can be the wrong ergonomic shape for a particular hand.
Material hierarchy is therefore context-dependent and subordinate to fit and use.
content.takeaway: The correct handle is the one whose whole design works for the person and environment.

question.prompt: A small-handed user dislikes rear-heavy knives but wants desert ironwood. What should staff do?

options.text: Test actual geometry and balance first.
Assume the rare wood will improve ergonomics automatically.
Ignore grip because material preference overrides balance.
Choose the longest handle to maximize wood content.

question.explanation: Material preference should be tested against actual balance and hand fit.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can carbon-fibre composite and G10 both be good yet feel very different?

options.text: One necessarily changes blade steel chemistry.
One automatically creates a single bevel.
One always absorbs more water than raw wood.
Layup, density, finish, contour and mass distribution

recovery_questions.explanation: Material family does not define the complete handle build.

questions.prompt: What makes a steel recommendation defensible?

options.text: Choosing the most famous steel name
Quoting only the highest HRC number
Explicit priorities and stated trade-offs
Ignoring sharpening tools and maintenance skill

questions.explanation: A defensible recommendation links evidence to the user's operating conditions.

questions.prompt: Which approach best avoids a handle-material shortcut?

options.text: Rank materials by rarity only.
Compare material, geometry, balance and care
Rank materials by density only.
Rank materials by gloss level only.

questions.explanation: Advanced evaluation uses the complete hand-interface system.

modules.title: Damascus & Layered Construction
modules.summary: Audit construction and marketing claims, then predict realistic edge evolution under differential wear.

lessons.title: Audit Damascus claims against construction evidence

content.lead: Advanced Damascus knowledge separates visual claim, construction route, working edge and historical terminology.
points: Clad Damascus may place patterned layers around a monosteel core; full Damascus can bring layered structure through the cutting region.
Pattern-welded, crucible-derived and surface-decorated patterns require different language because their mechanisms differ.
Performance claims must follow core/edge steel, heat treatment and geometry rather than visual layer count.
content.takeaway: A beautiful pattern is evidence of a pattern; performance needs additional evidence.

question.prompt: A clad blade has 101 patterned outer layers over a monosteel core. What mainly controls edge retention?

options.text: The outer layer count alone
The visual symmetry of the pattern
Core metallurgy and edge geometry
The handle material density

question.explanation: If the cutting edge is the core steel, its metallurgy and geometry dominate edge retention.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why is 'Damascus = sharper' an invalid general rule?

options.text: Sharpness is apex geometry, not a pattern label.
Damascus blades cannot be sharpened below 20 degrees.
Damascus always uses softer core steel.
Damascus patterns prevent burr formation.

recovery_questions.explanation: Construction category and apex quality are distinct variables.

lessons.title: Predict how differential wear evolves

content.lead: Advanced reasoning treats differential wear as a dynamic edge system affected by use and maintenance.
points: Layer hardness/composition differences can create uneven micro-wear; sliding cuts may benefit more from resulting texture than pure push cuts.
Aggressive sharpening can reset or mask the evolved texture; subsequent use rebuilds wear according to actual contact conditions.
Board hardness and food abrasiveness can accelerate overall edge wear even if bite remains useful.
content.takeaway: Predict bite, sharpness and maintenance separately over time.

question.prompt: A full-Damascus slicer retains bite but no longer push-cuts cleanly. What is the most coherent interpretation?

options.text: The knife has become sharper in every cutting mode.
Microtexture still supports sliding bite.
The handle has automatically shifted the balance forward.
The steel has increased its hardness during use.

question.explanation: Slicing bite can persist after peak push-cut sharpness declines.

recovery_questions.prompt: What could temporarily reduce the visible differential-wear effect at the edge?

options.text: Changing the handle colour
Increasing packaging humidity
A fresh sharpening that removes the evolved microtexture
Changing the tang from hidden to full without touching the blade

recovery_questions.explanation: Sharpening can reset edge topography; use then evolves it again.

questions.prompt: Which statement needs the most correction?

options.text: Layer count can describe construction complexity.
Core steel can dominate a clad blade's cutting edge behaviour.
Historical crucible Damascus is a different route from pattern welding.
Laser pattern means genuine layered Damascus.

questions.explanation: Surface decoration must not be reclassified as structural layering based on appearance.

questions.prompt: Which variable would most affect how fast differential texture develops?

options.text: Layer-wear contrast
Logo engraving font
Handle pin count
Box dimensions

questions.explanation: Differential wear is driven by material contrast under real abrasion/contact.

modules.title: Geometry & Bevels
modules.summary: Diagnose resistance, support and steering from interacting geometric variables, including maintenance-induced changes.

lessons.title: Diagnose cutting resistance from multiple geometric variables

content.lead: Advanced geometry separates apex sharpness, edge angle, thickness behind edge and blade-face wedging.
points: A keen apex can still cut poorly in dense food if thickness grows too quickly behind it.
A low edge angle improves initial penetration but can reduce support if steel/toughness and thickness are insufficient.
Convexity can add support and change food separation while a hollow can reduce material near the edge but also reduce support.
content.takeaway: Ask where resistance begins: apex, shoulder, face or food contact.

question.prompt: A knife starts a potato easily but then wedges halfway through. Which diagnosis is strongest?

options.text: The apex is necessarily completely dull.
The handle material is causing the food to split.
The steel has insufficient chromium for potatoes.
Behind-edge thickness and face geometry

question.explanation: Easy entry followed by wedging points beyond the apex to supporting geometry.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can thinning improve cutting even if the edge angle is unchanged?

options.text: It increases chromium in solution.
It reduces behind-edge material and wedging.
It changes a hidden tang into a full tang.
It raises the hardness automatically.

recovery_questions.explanation: Thinning changes the geometry supporting the edge rather than the edge angle itself.

lessons.title: Diagnose steering and asymmetry without erasing design

content.lead: Advanced maintenance distinguishes intentional asymmetry from accidental asymmetry introduced by sharpening.
points: Steering can arise from asymmetrical bevel proportions, unequal face geometry, food contact and user technique.
Repeated equal sharpening can move an intentionally offset edge toward centre; repeated one-sided work can create unintended offset.
On urasuki knives, reference lands provide the geometry needed to maintain the reverse correctly.
content.takeaway: Diagnose the source of steering before changing bevel ratios.

question.prompt: A formerly neutral 50/50 knife begins steering after many one-sided touch-ups. What is a plausible cause?

options.text: Sharpening has shifted the edge geometry asymmetrically.
The chromium content changed during storage.
The tang became longer with use.
The handle absorbed enough water to change bevel ratio.

question.explanation: Maintenance can create steering by changing edge position/proportions.

recovery_questions.prompt: A traditional single-bevel knife steers strongly for a left-handed user. What should staff check first?

options.text: Whether the handle contains enough carbon fibre
Whether the HRC is even or odd
Whether the blade has more than 60 Damascus layers
Whether the model's handed orientation matches the user's hand

recovery_questions.explanation: Strongly asymmetric specialist geometry is often orientation-dependent.

questions.prompt: Which observation best separates dullness from wedging?

options.text: Whether the handle is wood or G10
Whether the logo is centered
Where resistance begins in the cut
Whether the blade is stored in a saya

questions.explanation: Where resistance appears along the cut helps identify the geometric cause.

questions.prompt: What is the safest response to steering on an asymmetric knife?

options.text: Immediately convert both sides to a perfect 50/50 bevel.
Verify intended geometry before regrinding
Increase HRC through more sharpening passes.
Change the handle material first.

questions.explanation: Regrinding without diagnosis can erase intentional geometry.

modules.title: Knife Families & Ergonomics
modules.summary: Solve conflicting task briefs and diagnose fatigue through geometry, leverage and contact rather than subjective labels alone.

lessons.title: Solve complex knife-selection scenarios

content.lead: Advanced selection prioritizes competing tasks and identifies when one knife cannot optimally satisfy all of them.
points: A broad board-prep need, fine tip work and heavy bone impact point toward different geometries and may justify multiple tools.
Specialist knives should be recommended when their mechanical advantage matches recurring work, not because their silhouettes are distinctive.
The shortlist should explicitly state which tasks each candidate does well and which tasks remain outside its safe envelope.
content.takeaway: Sometimes the correct answer is two knives, not a compromised universal knife.

question.prompt: A customer wants one thin gyuto for vegetables and repeated heavy bone chopping. What is the best advanced recommendation?

options.text: Choose the hardest possible gyuto and use it for both.
Choose a thinner edge so bone impact feels easier.
Use separate tools for prep and bone impact.
Use the same gyuto but twist the blade to split joints.

question.explanation: The tasks require conflicting geometry/load tolerance, so tool separation is rational.

recovery_questions.prompt: When does a specialist knife earn its place in a recommendation?

options.text: When it solves a frequent important task.
Whenever its silhouette looks unusual.
Whenever it uses the most expensive steel.
Whenever it has the highest layer count.

recovery_questions.explanation: Specialization is valuable when matched to recurring work.

lessons.title: Diagnose fatigue from mass, grip and handle geometry

content.lead: Advanced ergonomics turns a complaint such as 'this knife is tiring' into testable causes.
points: Forward mass increases torque around a rear grip; moving to a pinch grip can reduce that lever arm but may expose a poor bolster transition.
A thick or angular handle can create local pressure even if balance is good; a smooth handle can feel insecure when wet even if its size fits.
Fatigue can come from total mass, rotational inertia, grip force, wrist posture or repeated motion; changing steel grade alone may solve none of them.
content.takeaway: Translate subjective feel into geometry, leverage and contact-pressure hypotheses.

question.prompt: A knife feels tiring only when held at the rear of the handle, but comfortable in a pinch grip. What is the leading hypothesis?

options.text: The steel becomes softer when held farther back.
Forward mass increases the rear-grip lever arm.
The tang changes length between grips.
The edge angle changes automatically with hand position.

question.explanation: Grip position changes leverage relative to the same mass distribution.

recovery_questions.prompt: A well-balanced knife still creates a hot spot on the index finger. What should be examined?

options.text: Only the centre of mass
Only blade HRC
Bolster/handle contour and local pressure
Only Damascus layer count

recovery_questions.explanation: Balance can be good while local geometry remains uncomfortable.

questions.prompt: Which shortlist is most useful?

options.text: Every knife in the store sorted by price
Only the most prestigious steel grades
Only knives with matching handle colours
A few task-fit knives with explicit trade-offs

questions.explanation: A shortlist should reduce uncertainty by holding function constant and comparing meaningful differences.

questions.prompt: Which test best validates an ergonomic recommendation?

options.text: Compare task-fit knives in natural grip
Choose the lightest knife without handling it.
Choose the longest handle from specifications.
Choose the densest handle material automatically.

questions.explanation: Direct comparison under the user's real grip is the strongest ergonomic evidence available in store.

modules.title: Cutting Techniques
modules.summary: Diagnose cutting faults from interacting variables and set safe boundaries for specialist techniques.

lessons.title: Diagnose poor cutting from path, geometry and food response

content.lead: Advanced technique diagnosis separates edge sharpness, motion, food stability and blade profile before correcting anything.
points: Cracking in dense food may indicate wedging or too little slicing travel; incomplete board contact may indicate movement/curvature mismatch.
Dragging or tearing delicate food can come from dullness, short sawing, excess pressure or unsuitable edge finish.
Technique correction should change one variable at a time to identify the actual cause.
content.takeaway: Diagnose first; then choose the smallest effective correction.

question.prompt: A sharp slicer tears salmon only when the user makes short back-and-forth strokes. What is the best correction?

options.text: Increase downward force while keeping short strokes.
Twist the blade slightly during each pass.
Move the food closer to the body without changing the path.
Use a longer controlled draw that exploits the blade length.

question.explanation: The symptom is movement-dependent; the slicer geometry is designed for long draw cuts.

recovery_questions.prompt: A nakiri leaves thin skins uncut only during wide rocking. What is the leading explanation?

options.text: Its steel lacks enough cobalt.
Poor contact during wide rocking
Its handle needs more oil.
Its tang is too short.

recovery_questions.explanation: Movement and edge curvature are mismatched.

lessons.title: Set boundaries for high-skill specialist techniques

content.lead: Advanced competence includes knowing when explanation is insufficient and demonstration or supervised practice is required.
points: In-hand cutting, fish butchery and fine joint work place the edge near hands/body or hard anatomy and require precise spatial control.
A specialist blade can enable a technique but does not make unsafe positioning safe.
Training should progress from slow path control and stable work to speed, not the reverse.
content.takeaway: Advanced skill includes refusing to improvise a hazardous technique.

question.prompt: A trainee wants to imitate fast in-hand peeling after reading the description once. What is the best instruction?

options.text: Use supervised demonstration and slow controlled practice before speed.
Speed up immediately so the blade spends less time near the hand.
Use a larger knife because mass improves safety.
Hold the food closer to the body for stability.

question.explanation: High-risk specialist movement should be learned through controlled demonstration, not imitation at speed.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why does a specialist knife not make a hazardous load safe?

options.text: Specialist knives cannot be sharpened.
Specialist knives contain no tough steel.
Specialist knives are only decorative.
Specialist geometry still has load limits.

recovery_questions.explanation: Specialization narrows the correct use; it does not remove mechanical limits.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest diagnostic clue that technique, not sharpness, is the main problem?

options.text: The blade has a visible logo.
The handle is made of wood.
Performance changes with the movement path.
The knife has a full tang.

questions.explanation: A symptom that follows a particular motion points strongly toward technique/geometry interaction.

questions.prompt: Which sign says a technique should be stopped and reassessed?

options.text: The cut proceeds smoothly with a clear path.
Unexpected force, twisting or unstable hand position
The supporting hand remains protected.
The board and food remain stable.

questions.explanation: Unexpected force or instability is diagnostic information, not a cue to push harder.

modules.title: Safe Use & Handling
modules.summary: Analyse incidents as systems failures and design layered controls that remain reliable under distraction.

lessons.title: Analyse incidents as systems failures

content.lead: Advanced safety reconstructs the chain of conditions that made an incident possible.
points: An injury can combine board movement, poor food stabilization, wrong tool, excessive force and exposed supporting fingers.
The last visible action is not always the root cause; workstation and task design may have created the problem earlier.
Corrective action should remove upstream causes rather than merely telling users to be more careful.
content.takeaway: Ask what made the unsafe action likely, not only who made it.

question.prompt: A cook slips while forcing a rolling squash with a thin slicer. What is the strongest root-cause analysis?

options.text: The only cause is that the cook moved too slowly.
The only cause is insufficient blade hardness.
Multiple upstream controls failed.
The only cause is the handle material.

question.explanation: System analysis identifies multiple interacting precursors rather than one final action.

recovery_questions.prompt: Which corrective action is strongest after repeated board-slip incidents?

options.text: Standardize and verify non-slip board setup.
Tell staff to grip knives harder.
Increase cutting speed targets.
Use heavier knives on every task.

recovery_questions.explanation: Engineering/setup controls reduce reliance on moment-to-moment vigilance.

lessons.title: Design layered controls for knife handling

content.lead: Advanced handling design uses equipment, layout, communication and training together.
points: Knife storage should make sharp edges visible/predictable and physically separated from hands and hard objects.
Transport controls should secure the blade and define orientation before movement begins.
Passing protocols should combine handle-first orientation with eye/contact confirmation rather than assuming the receiver is ready.
content.takeaway: Good safety survives distraction because the system itself supports correct behaviour.

question.prompt: Which storage redesign best reduces both injury and edge damage?

options.text: A deeper loose drawer with more utensils
Fitted storage that isolates each edge
A towel placed over loose knives
A metal tray where blades can move freely

question.explanation: Physical separation and fixed orientation protect both people and edges.

recovery_questions.prompt: What makes a knife-passing protocol robust?

options.text: Speed so the transfer ends quickly
Passing blade-first so the edge remains visible
Defined orientation plus receiver confirmation
Relying only on individual experience

recovery_questions.explanation: Communication and geometry together reduce transfer ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Why is 'be careful' a weak standalone corrective action?

options.text: Carefulness always reduces steel hardness.
It changes board material chemistry.
It alters the bevel ratio.
It leaves hazards unchanged.

questions.explanation: Reliable safety comes from controlling conditions as well as behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which control is least dependent on perfect attention?

options.text: A fitted guard that isolates the edge
Remembering not to reach into a mixed utensil drawer
Telling everyone to move more slowly
Assuming experienced staff will notice hidden blades

questions.explanation: Physical controls remain effective even when attention is imperfect.

modules.title: Care & Cutting Boards
modules.summary: Design board strategy across the operating lifecycle and diagnose specific corrosion, edge and handle failure modes.

lessons.title: Choose board strategy for edge, hygiene and environment

content.lead: Advanced board selection weighs knife population, cleaning regime, edge cost and environmental constraints.
points: A professional kitchen may rationally choose resilient synthetic boards for sanitation workflow even if high-quality wood is edge-friendly.
Very hard presentation surfaces should be separated from actual cutting surfaces in workflow design.
Replacement interval matters: deeply scarred plastic or damaged boards can lose hygiene/stability advantages.
content.takeaway: The board system includes material, condition, cleaning and replacement policy.

question.prompt: A kitchen sanitizes aggressively and uses many thin hard edges. Which board strategy is most coherent?

options.text: Use glass everywhere because it sanitizes easily.
Use stone because it cannot absorb moisture.
Keep deeply scarred boards indefinitely to reduce cost.
Resilient sanitation-compatible professional board

question.explanation: The choice must satisfy both sanitation workflow and edge friendliness.

recovery_questions.prompt: Why can board condition matter as much as board material?

options.text: Wear changes the knife's HRC.
Grooves or warping can compromise stability/hygiene
Scratches turn plastic into glass.
Warping increases chromium in the blade.

recovery_questions.explanation: A suitable material can become unsuitable when condition deteriorates.

lessons.title: Diagnose corrosion and edge failure before prescribing care

content.lead: Advanced maintenance separates symptoms that need cleaning, honing, sharpening, repair or retirement.
points: Orange active rust, pitting, stable patina and superficial staining need different interpretations and responses.
Rolling, chipping, blunting and wire-edge failure create different edge symptoms and require different correction.
Handle cracks, loose scales or structural play are not solved by blade oil or sharpening.
content.takeaway: Treat the failure mode, not the word 'dull' or 'rusty'.

question.prompt: A knife feels dull, but the apex is visibly rolled rather than abraded away. What is a reasonable first maintenance step?

options.text: Appropriate light realignment/honing, then reassess the edge
Heavy reprofiling immediately
Oil the blade and ignore the edge
Increase HRC through polishing

question.explanation: A rolled apex can sometimes be realigned before deciding whether abrasive sharpening is needed.

recovery_questions.prompt: A stainless blade develops small deep pits after salty wet storage. What is the most accurate diagnosis?

options.text: Healthy protective patina identical to carbon steel
Normal burr formation from sharpening
A handle-balance issue
Localized pitting corrosion despite stainless composition

recovery_questions.explanation: Stainless is corrosion-resistant, not immune to chloride/wet-storage pitting.

questions.prompt: Which metric best captures total board cost for a knife program?

options.text: Purchase price only
Board colour only
Total lifecycle cost
Maximum hardness only

questions.explanation: Advanced selection considers operational lifecycle rather than purchase price alone.

questions.prompt: Which symptom calls for structural repair rather than edge maintenance?

options.text: A small sharpening burr
Loose handle scales
A slightly rolled apex
A normal dark carbon-steel patina

questions.explanation: Handle movement is an assembly problem, not an edge-maintenance problem.

modules.title: Sharpening & Edge Maintenance
modules.summary: Select the correct scale of geometry correction and diagnose burr, stone and abrasive failure modes from evidence.

lessons.title: Separate sharpening, thinning and reprofiling

content.lead: Advanced sharpening chooses the scale of intervention: restore apex, correct local geometry, thin behind the edge or reprofile deliberately.
points: Sharpening the edge bevel restores the apex; thinning changes thickness behind the edge; reprofiling changes angles/shape more substantially.
Repeated sharpening can thicken a blade behind the edge over time as the apex moves into thicker material.
Local low spots or recurve require controlled geometry correction rather than indiscriminate heavy grinding.
content.takeaway: Choose the smallest intervention that fixes the diagnosed geometry.

question.prompt: A knife is sharp at the apex but now wedges badly after years of sharpening. What intervention is most relevant?

options.text: Polish the handle to reduce friction.
Increase the final edge angle further.
Assess behind-edge thinning needs.
Add more oil to the blade surface.

question.explanation: Repeated edge sharpening can move the apex into thicker material, creating a thinning problem rather than an apex problem.

recovery_questions.prompt: When is reprofiling more appropriate than routine sharpening?

options.text: When edge geometry needs substantial restoration
Whenever a tiny burr is detected
Whenever the blade is stainless
Whenever a fine finishing stone is available

recovery_questions.explanation: Reprofiling deliberately changes geometry beyond normal apex maintenance.

lessons.title: Diagnose burr, abrasive and stone failures

content.lead: Advanced sharpening identifies why an edge fails a test rather than simply adding more strokes.
points: A wire edge may pass paper then fold in food; overpressure can create large burrs and unstable apex geometry.
A dished stone changes local contact and can unintentionally convex or alter bevel geometry.
An abrasive that is too slow for hard carbides can encourage excess pressure, while an overly aggressive abrasive can remove unnecessary steel if poorly controlled.
content.takeaway: Edge symptoms, stone condition and abrasive match form one diagnostic system.

question.prompt: An edge cuts paper perfectly immediately after sharpening but folds after a few tomato slices. What is the strongest suspicion?

options.text: The tang is too long.
A remaining wire edge
The handle is too dense.
The board contains too much chromium.

question.explanation: Short-lived sharpness after sharpening is a classic reason to inspect burr removal and apex stability.

recovery_questions.prompt: A flat bevel slowly becomes convex despite a steady hand. What equipment issue should be checked?

options.text: Handle oil viscosity
Blade logo depth
Stone dishing
Packaging foam density

recovery_questions.explanation: A non-flat stone changes contact geometry even with consistent hand motion.

questions.prompt: Why should thinning be planned carefully on a clad or patterned blade?

options.text: It always changes the steel grade.
It converts the tang type.
It guarantees higher corrosion resistance.
It changes face geometry.

questions.explanation: Thinning is a blade-face geometry operation with cosmetic and structural consequences.

questions.prompt: A high-carbide steel barely abrades, so the user presses much harder. What is the better correction?

options.text: Use a more efficient carbide-capable abrasive.
Continue increasing pressure until the stone deforms.
Raise the edge angle solely to make abrasion faster.
Soak every stone overnight regardless of manufacturer instructions.

questions.explanation: Abrasive mismatch should be solved with abrasive choice, not uncontrolled force.
